pos: v.t. (to bear or conduct to a place; rendering Hebrew bo in the causative, Greek agō, pherō)
etymology: Saxon bringan, to bear along. In Scripture the verb is overwhelmingly God's: He brings out, brings in, brings forth, and brings to pass.
biblical_def: To bring is to carry a thing or a person from where they are to where they must be, and in Scripture the great subject of the verb is God. He brought Israel out: “Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt” (Exo 3:10) — and note that Moses is sent, but the bringing is the LORD's work through him. He brings the believer's committed way to its end: “Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass” (Psa 37:5), which is the whole doctrine of providence in a single verb. He brings the dead with Christ: “them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him” (1Th 4:14). And He brings sons home through suffering: “in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings” (Heb 2:10). Salvation, in Hebrews' language, is a bringing — a company of sons conducted to glory behind a Captain who went the road first. Man does not bring himself. He is brought.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bring as to fetch, to bear from a distant place, to convey or remove to a nearer place, and to procure or cause to come.
webster_full: BRING, v.t. To fetch; to bear, convey or lead from a distant to a nearer place.
2. To produce; to procure as a cause; to draw to.
3. To attract or draw along.
4. To cause to come; to cause to proceed from a distant place, in company, or at the same time.
To bring to pass, to effect; to accomplish.
scriptures: Exo 3:10
Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt.
Psa 37:5
Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.
For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him.
Heb 2:10
For it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings.
corruption_summary: A generation trained to bring itself — to self-actualise, self-deliver, self-make — has no grammar left for a salvation in which the sinner is the object of the verb and God its subject.
corruption_paragraphs: The plainest evidence of a doctrine is who governs the verbs, and modern religion has quietly changed the subject. God's part becomes offering, enabling, or accompanying; man's part becomes the actual bringing. But Hebrews says the Father is bringing many sons unto glory, Psalm 37 says He shall bring it to pass, and Exodus says He brought Israel out with a stretched-out arm. Where the verb is handed back to man, assurance goes with it, because a soul that brought itself this far must now bring itself the rest of the way.

The pastoral consequence is exhaustion. Committing a way to the LORD and trusting Him to bring it to pass is rest; managing outcomes on His behalf is not. And the promise is not that God brings the believer round the sufferings — Hebrews 2:10 says the Captain Himself was made perfect through them, which means the road to glory runs through the very trouble the believer keeps asking to be brought around. He brings sons home; He does not always bring them the way they would have chosen.
roots_summary: Hebrew bo (H935) in the causative, to cause to come or bring in; Greek agō (G71), to lead, and pherō (G5342), to bear — the verbs of exodus and of glory.
roots_lines: Hebrew bo (H935) — to come or go; in the hiphil, to bring in, bring out, bring to pass; the standard verb of the exodus (Exo 3:8).
Hebrew yatsa (H3318) — in the hiphil, to bring forth, lead out; “I brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians” (Exo 6:7).
Greek agō (G71) — to lead or bring; Hebrews' “bringing many sons unto glory” (Heb 2:10).
usage: “He shall bring it to pass” — providence stated as a promise to the committed way.
“Bringing many sons unto glory” — salvation as a conducted journey behind a Captain.
“Them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him” — the grave does not lose the escort.

pos: v.t. (to place, fix, or appoint; rendering Hebrew shith, sim, Greek tithēmi, histemi)
etymology: Saxon settan, causative of sit — to cause to sit, hence to fix in place. Scripture uses it for what God establishes and for what a man deliberately fixes his heart upon.
biblical_def: To set is to put a thing deliberately in a place and leave it there, and Scripture uses it for both God's establishing and man's resolving. God sets a rescued man on solid ground: “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings” (Psa 40:2). God set a joy before His Son: “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Heb 12:2) — the same verb twice, the joy set before Him and the Son now set down, the enduring bracketed by two divine placements. Answering this, the believer is commanded to set: “Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth” (Col 3:2), and David testifies, “I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved” (Psa 16:8). Setting is therefore the deliberate act by which a soul decides in advance where it will look. It is not a mood that visits; it is a placement a man makes and keeps.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines set as to put or place, to fix firmly, to appoint or assign, and to fix the affection or heart upon an object.
webster_full: SET, v.t. To put or place; to fix or cause to rest in a standing posture.
2. To put or place in its proper or natural posture.
3. To fix; to make fast or firm.
4. To appoint; to assign; as, to set a time.
To set the heart on, to fix the desires on; to love or covet.
scriptures: Psa 40:2
He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.
Heb 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
Col 3:2
Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
Psa 16:8
I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.
corruption_summary: Devotion has been redefined as feeling that arrives rather than affection a man sets, which leaves the believer waiting on his moods for what Scripture commands him to do on purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: “Set your affection on things above” is an imperative, and imperatives assume the thing can be done whether or not one feels like doing it. Much modern piety assumes the reverse: that love for God is a weather system, and that the honest response to a cold heart is to wait for warmth. Scripture treats the affections as steerable — they follow what a man deliberately puts before his eyes. David does not report a feeling; he reports a placement: I have set the LORD always before me. The feeling followed, and so did the stability.

Hebrews shows the same mechanism in the Lord Himself. He endured the cross for a joy that was set before Him — that is, He held a future gladness in view and let it carry Him through present shame. This is not stoicism, which denies the shame, nor is it sentiment, which waits for the shame to stop hurting. It is a deliberate setting of the mind on what is real above, and it is exactly what Colossians commands of every believer under pressure.
roots_summary: Hebrew shith (H7896) and sim (H7760), to put, place, appoint; Greek tithēmi (G5087), to lay or set, and phroneō (G5426), to set the mind upon.
roots_lines: Hebrew shith (H7896) — to put, set, appoint; “I have set the LORD always before me” (Psa 16:8).
Hebrew sim (H7760) — to place, establish, constitute; used of setting a king and setting a boundary.
Greek phroneō (G5426) — to be minded, to set the mind or affection on; the imperative of Col 3:2.
usage: “Set my feet upon a rock” — deliverance described as a placement God makes.
“Set your affection on things above” — devotion commanded as a deliberate act.
“For the joy that was set before him endured the cross” — the Lord's own method under shame.

pos: v.t. & adj. (to unclose, to unfasten; rendering Hebrew pathach, Greek anoigō)
etymology: Saxon openian, from up — to lift or raise, as a lid is lifted. Scripture's decisive openings are all God's: hands, lips, hearts, and doors.
biblical_def: Almost every opening that matters in Scripture is done by God. He opens His hand in providence: “Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing” (Psa 145:16) — every creature that eats today eats out of an opened hand. He opens a mouth for praise, and the penitent knows he cannot do it himself: “O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise” (Psa 51:15), the plea of a man whose sin had shut him up. He opens the heart, and Luke states it as flatly as it can be stated: Lydia heard, “whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul” (Act 16:14) — the preaching was heard by many, the heart was opened by One. And He opens doors no man can shut: “behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength” (Rev 3:8). The pattern is uniform and it is the doctrine of grace in a verb. What is shut in man — hand, mouth, heart, way — is opened from outside.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines open as to unclose, to set apart from anything that encloses, to remove any fastening, and figuratively to disclose or make plain.
webster_full: OPEN, v.t. To unclose; to unbar; to unlock; to remove any fastening or cover and set open.
2. To break the seal of a letter and unfold it.
3. To begin; to make the first exhibition.
4. To show; to bring to view or knowledge.
5. To make plain; to explain; to disclose.
scriptures: Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing.
O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise.
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
Rev 3:8
I know thy works: behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name.
corruption_summary: The opening of the heart has been reassigned to the sinner — a decision he makes, a door he unlatches from within — where Luke says plainly that the Lord opened Lydia's heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The most quoted picture in modern evangelism is a door with the handle only on the inside. Acts 16:14 says the opposite, and it says it about a woman who was already worshipping God and already listening: she heard, and the Lord opened her heart, and then she attended. Grammar settles the doctrine. The Lord is the subject, the heart is the object, and attending to Paul's words is the result, not the cause. This is effectual calling, and it is why the dictionary holds monergism — not as a preference among schemes, but because the verbs in the text run that way.

The practical fruit is neither passivity nor presumption. Because God opens hands, the believer prays for bread rather than trusting the supply chain. Because God opens lips, the guilty man does not wait until he feels articulate before confessing. Because God opens hearts, the preacher preaches to hard men without despair, and gives Him the credit when they soften. And because God opens doors, a church with little strength may still find a field no man can shut against it.
roots_summary: Hebrew pathach (H6605), to open, loosen, set free; Greek anoigō (G455), to open — the hand of providence, the lips of praise, the heart, and the door.
roots_lines: Hebrew pathach (H6605) — to open, unfasten, loose; “Thou openest thine hand” (Psa 145:16) and “open thou my lips” (Psa 51:15).
Greek anoigō (G455) — to open; the opened heart of Lydia (Act 16:14) and the opened door of Rev 3:8.
Greek dianoigō (G1272) — to open thoroughly; used of the Lord opening the scriptures and the understanding (Luk 24:45).
usage: “Thou openest thine hand” — daily bread traced to a divine gesture.
“Whose heart the Lord opened” — conversion in the passive voice.
“I have set before thee an open door” — opportunity given to a church of little strength.

pos: v.t. (to close, to bar; rendering Hebrew sagar, Greek kleiō)
etymology: Saxon scyttan, to bar or bolt. In Scripture the shutting is God's prerogative — sometimes the tenderest mercy, sometimes the last judgment.
biblical_def: To shut in Scripture is an act of authority, and the same hand does it in mercy and in judgment. In mercy: when Noah and his household were aboard and the beasts gathered, “the LORD shut him in” (Gen 7:16) — the door of the ark was closed from outside, by God, and no wave and no neighbour could open it. In judgment: the foolish virgins went to buy, “and while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut” (Mat 25:10). Christ holds the authority absolutely: “he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth” (Rev 3:7). And there is a shutting the believer is commanded to do himself — “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6) — the deliberate closing out of an audience so that prayer has only one hearer. Shut in by God, shut out by God, shutting the door on ourselves for prayer: the word covers the safest place in Scripture and the most terrible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shut as to close so as to hinder ingress or egress, to bar, to preclude, to exclude, and to confine.
webster_full: SHUT, v.t. To close so as to prevent ingress or egress; as, to shut a door or gate.
2. To prohibit; to bar; to forbid entrance into.
3. To preclude; to exclude.
4. To close, as the hand or the eyes.
To shut in, to enclose; to confine.
scriptures: Gen 7:16
And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in.
And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut.
Rev 3:7

And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write; These things saith he that is holy, he that is true, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth;
Mat 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
corruption_summary: A shut door is now treated as the one thing love could never do, so the closing of Matthew 25 is preached as a parable about preparedness in general and never as a door that actually shuts.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine at stake is finality. Universalism in its various forms — and the softer assumption, far more common in the pews, that God will surely let everyone in eventually — requires that no door ever truly shuts. Our Lord's own parable ends with a shut door and a refused entry, and He told it to religious people. Revelation grounds the authority in His hands alone: what He shuts, no man opens. Sentiment cannot pick that lock, and preaching that quietly promises it can is not kindness.

Set beside it, Genesis 7:16 is one of the most comforting sentences in the Bible. Noah did not have to hold the door. God shut him in, and the same shutting that sealed out the flood sealed him in with the promise. That is the believer's security — kept by the power of God, not by his own grip on the latch. The shut door of Matthew 25 and the shut door of Genesis 7 are the same divine act seen from opposite sides, and every soul will know it from one side or the other.
roots_summary: Hebrew sagar (H5462), to shut, close, deliver up; Greek kleiō (G2808), to shut or lock — the ark's door, the marriage door, and the key of David.
roots_lines: Hebrew sagar (H5462) — to shut, close up, enclose; “the LORD shut him in” (Gen 7:16).
Greek kleiō (G2808) — to shut, bar; the shut door of Mat 25:10 and the authority of Rev 3:7.
The same verb underlies shutting up the kingdom of heaven against men (Mat 23:13) — a shutting men attempt and will answer for.
usage: “The LORD shut him in” — the safest sentence in the flood narrative.
“And the door was shut” — the parable ends where sentiment refuses to go.
“When thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father” — prayer with the audience removed.

pos: v.t. (to extend, stretch out, or lay open; rendering Hebrew paras, Greek strōnnumi)
etymology: Saxon sprædan, to stretch out. The characteristic biblical gestures are spread hands in prayer, spread wings in protection, and a spread letter in crisis.
biblical_def: To spread is to stretch a thing out to its full extent, and Scripture puts the verb to three great uses. It describes God's protection: “He spread a cloud for a covering; and fire to give light in the night” (Psa 105:39) — the wilderness canopy that shaded by day and lit by dark; and the eagle image of Deuteronomy, which “spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings” (Deu 32:11). It describes God's long patience with rebels, in one of the most affecting lines in the prophets: “I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people, which walketh in a way that was not good, after their own thoughts” (Isa 65:2) — the posture of appeal, held out all day, to people walking the other way. And it describes what a believer does with bad news: Hezekiah “received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it: and Hezekiah went up unto the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD” (Isa 37:14). He did not answer the letter; he opened it flat in the presence of God. That is prayer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spread as to extend in length and breadth, to expand, to stretch, to open and lay out, and to cause to be more widely known.
webster_full: SPREAD, v.t. To extend in length and breadth, or in breadth only; to stretch or expand to a broader surface.
2. To set; to place; to pitch; as, to spread a tent.
3. To cover by extending something.
4. To extend; to shoot to a greater length in every direction.
5. To divulge; to publish; to cause to be more extensively known.
scriptures: He spread a cloud for a covering; and fire to give light in the night.
As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings:
Isa 65:2
I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people, which walketh in a way that was not good, after their own thoughts;
And Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it: and Hezekiah went up unto the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD.
corruption_summary: Prayer has been reduced to explaining a problem to God or to talking oneself calm; Hezekiah's spread letter is the older and better method — the trouble opened flat, unedited, in the house of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Two habits crowd out the spread letter. The first is management: the crisis is analysed, options are ranked, and prayer arrives at the end as a blessing on the plan already chosen. The second is therapeutic self-soothing, in which prayer is valued for what it does to the one praying and God's actual involvement becomes optional. Hezekiah does neither. He carries the enemy's own words into the temple, lays them open, and asks the LORD to read them — and it is the LORD, not Hezekiah, who answers Rabshakeh. <!-- voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic frame to reject it -->

Isaiah 65:2 guards this from becoming a technique. The hands spread all day are God's, held out to people who kept walking after their own thoughts — which means the initiative in every real prayer was His before it was ours. Paul quotes that verse in Romans 10 of Israel's unbelief, so the picture is not a sentimental one: a God who spreads out His hands all day is a God whose patience is real and whose rejection, when it finally comes, is just.
roots_summary: Hebrew paras (H6566), to spread out, stretch forth; Greek strōnnumi (G4766), to spread or strew — the covering cloud, the spread wings, the spread hands, the spread letter.
roots_lines: Hebrew paras (H6566) — to spread out, stretch forth; the spread hands of Isa 65:2 and Solomon's spread hands at the temple dedication (1Ki 8:22).
Hebrew paras is also used of the eagle spreading her wings over the young (Deu 32:11) — the same gesture, protection instead of appeal.
Greek strōnnumi (G4766) — to spread or strew; garments spread in the way at the triumphal entry (Mat 21:8).
usage: “He spread a cloud for a covering” — providence as shade by day and light by night.
“I have spread out my hands all the day” — the posture of a rejected God.
“Spread it before the LORD” — Hezekiah's method with a threatening letter.

pos: v.t. & v.i. (to agitate, to cause to tremble; rendering Hebrew ra'ash, Greek seiō, saleuō)
etymology: Saxon sceacan, to move violently to and fro. Scripture's shakings are deliberate divine acts that test what is founded and remove what is not.
biblical_def: God shakes on purpose, and Hebrews explains the purpose. Quoting Haggai — “Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land” (Hag 2:6) — the writer says, “Whose voice then shook the earth: but now he hath promised, saying, Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven” (Heb 12:26), and draws the conclusion that the shaking removes what can be shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain. Shaking is therefore not destruction for its own sake; it is a sorting. There is also a shaking of blessing and confirmation: after the church prayed, “the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost” (Act 4:31) — God answering a prayer for boldness by moving the building. And there is the shaking of generous measure: “good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over” (Luk 6:38), the grain settled by shaking so that more can be added. Judgment, confirmation, and generosity all reach for the same verb.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shake as to cause to move with quick vibrations, to agitate, to make to totter or tremble, and to throw down by a violent motion.
webster_full: SHAKE, v.t. To cause to move with quick vibrations; to move rapidly one way and the other; to agitate.
2. To make to totter or tremble.
3. To throw down by a violent motion; as, to shake down fruit.
4. To move from firmness; to weaken the stability of; to endanger; to threaten to overthrow.
5. To drive from a resolution, or to cause to waver.
scriptures: Hag 2:6
For thus saith the LORD of hosts; Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land;
Whose voice then shook the earth: but now he hath promised, saying, Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven.
Act 4:31
And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.
Luk 6:38

Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.
corruption_summary: Upheaval is read as evidence that God has lost control, when Hebrews presents the shaking as His own deliberate sorting of what will stand from what was never founded.
corruption_paragraphs: When institutions fall, reputations collapse, and long-settled certainties give way, the reflex of unbelief is to conclude that no one is steering. Hebrews 12 makes the shaking itself an act of the same voice that spoke at Sinai, and gives its purpose: the removing of what is made, that the things which cannot be shaken may remain. A believer watching things fall is watching a divine sifting, not a divine absence — and the practical question is never why God allowed the shaking but what in one's own life was resting on shakable ground.

The chapter's conclusion is not stoic endurance but worship: wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear. The unshakable thing already given is a kingdom. So Acts 4 fits: the church prays under threat, the room shakes, and what comes out of it is boldness in speech. God shakes the walls and steadies the men.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'ash (H7493), to quake, shake, tremble; Greek seiō (G4579) and saleuō (G4531), to shake or agitate — the sorting of what stands.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'ash (H7493) — to quake or shake; “I will shake the heavens, and the earth” (Hag 2:6).
Greek seiō (G4579) — to shake, agitate; the root behind seismos, an earthquake.
Greek saleuō (G4531) — to shake or make to totter; used in Heb 12:27 of the things that are shaken and removed.
usage: “Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven” — the last sorting announced in advance.
“The place was shaken where they were assembled” — God answering a prayer for boldness.
“Pressed down, and shaken together, and running over” — measure settled so more can be given.

pos: v.t. (to pull off or out with force; rendering Hebrew nathash, nasal, Greek exaireō, harpazō)
etymology: Saxon pluccian, to pull sharply. The word carries violence — nothing is plucked gently — and Scripture uses it for both mortification and rescue.
biblical_def: Pluck is a violent word, and Scripture keeps the violence. Our Lord uses it of mortifying sin: “And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell” (Mat 5:29). The comparison is not between a hard life and an easy one but between a maimed life and hell, and on that scale the amputation is bargain. He also uses it of security, and there the violence is on the other side: “I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand” (Joh 10:28) — a hand no force can pry open. Zechariah gives the third use, the plucking that is pure rescue: of Joshua the high priest standing filthy before the Angel, the LORD asks, “is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?” (Zec 3:2) — a half-burnt stick snatched from the coals, which is what every saved sinner is. Pluck out the offending member; you cannot be plucked out of His hand; you were plucked out of the fire.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pluck as to pull with sudden force or effort, to pull off, to strip by plucking, and to snatch away.
webster_full: PLUCK, v.t. To pull with sudden force or effort, or to pull off, out or from, with a twitch.
2. To strip by plucking; as, to pluck a fowl.
To pluck away, to pull away, or to separate by pulling; to tear away.
To pluck out, to draw out suddenly or to tear out.
scriptures: Mat 5:29
And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
Zec 3:2
And the LORD said unto Satan, The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan; even the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?
Isa 65:2
I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people, which walketh in a way that was not good, after their own thoughts;
corruption_summary: Mortification has been softened into management — boundaries, moderation, balance — where Christ prescribed amputation, and the softening is defended in the name of a kindness He never offered.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 5:29 is routinely handled as hyperbole and then handled no further, as though naming a figure of speech dismissed the demand. The figure is real; the demand is literal in force. Christ assumes there will be occasions of sin so bound to a man's ordinary life that removing them will feel like losing an eye, and He commands the removal anyway, on the plain ground that hell is worse. Counsel that only ever recommends moderation to a man in the grip of a besetting sin has quietly decided that hell is not really the alternative.

But mortification is never preached alone in Scripture, and this is where John 10 belongs. The believer cuts off the right hand precisely because he cannot be cut out of Christ's hand — security is the ground of severity, not its rival. And Zechariah 3 supplies the tone: the man being cleansed is a brand plucked from the fire, filthy garments and all, with Satan standing at his right hand to resist him and the LORD rebuking Satan on his behalf. That is the atmosphere in which amputation is possible.
roots_summary: Hebrew nathash (H5428), to pluck up by the roots, and nasal (H5337), to snatch away or deliver; Greek exaireō (G1807), to pluck out, and harpazō (G726), to seize by force.
roots_lines: Hebrew nathash (H5428) — to pluck up, root out; Jeremiah's commission to pluck up and to plant (Jer 1:10).
Hebrew nasal (H5337) — to snatch away, deliver, rescue; behind the brand plucked from the fire (Zec 3:2; Amo 4:11).
Greek harpazō (G726) — to seize, snatch away by force; “neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand” (Joh 10:28).
usage: “Pluck it out, and cast it from thee” — mortification measured against hell, not against comfort.
“Neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand” — a grip no force can open.
“A brand plucked out of the fire” — the standing description of a saved sinner.

pos: v.t. & v.i. (to set the foot upon, to trample; rendering Hebrew darak, Greek pateō)
etymology: Saxon tredan, to step. Treading is the posture of the conqueror and the labour of the winepress — and Scripture joins the two in one figure.
biblical_def: To tread is to put the foot down in mastery, and Scripture gives the verb to Christ before it gives it to the church. In Isaiah He speaks alone: “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury” (Isa 63:3), and the Revelation repeats it — “he treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God” (Rev 19:15). Wrath is a work, and the Lord does it Himself, without help. Only after that does the verb descend to His people, and always as a derived authority: “Behold, I give unto you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy: and nothing shall by any means hurt you” (Luk 10:19), and the psalm behind it, “Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet” (Psa 91:13). The believer's treading is not his own strength but the promise of Genesis 3:15 working out under the feet of those who belong to the Seed — the God of peace bruising Satan under their feet shortly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tread as to set the foot, to walk or go, to press under the foot, to trample in contempt, and to crush under the feet.
webster_full: TREAD, v.i. To set the foot; as, fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
2. To walk or go.
TREAD, v.t. To step or walk on.
2. To press under the foot; to trample in contempt.
3. To crush under the foot; to trample in hatred or revenge.
scriptures: Isa 63:3

I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.

And out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword, that with it he should smite the nations: and he shall rule them with a rod of iron: and he treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God.
Behold, I give unto you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy: and nothing shall by any means hurt you.
Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet.
corruption_summary: The winepress has been quietly retired as unworthy of God, and with it the doctrine that wrath is His personal, deliberate work — leaving a God who is never angry and a cross that answers nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 63 is among the most avoided passages in modern preaching, and the avoidance is doctrinal rather than aesthetic. If God does not personally tread the winepress — if wrath is only the impersonal outworking of bad choices, a mechanism rather than a disposition — then the cross is not propitiation, because there was no wrath to propitiate. Every attempt to keep a loving God by removing an angry one ends by removing the atonement, since substitution requires a real penalty really borne. The dictionary holds penal substitution, and Isaiah 63 is one of the reasons.

The other half of the passage is that He trod it alone: of the people there was none with me. No creature assisted, and no creature could. That is why Luke 10 is a gift and not an achievement — the disciples return rejoicing that the devils are subject to them, and the Lord immediately redirects their joy to their names written in heaven. Treading on serpents is delegated authority, and delegated authority is never a ground for boasting.
roots_summary: Hebrew darak (H1869), to tread, bend a bow, march; Greek pateō (G3961), to tread or trample — the winepress of wrath and the promised authority over the serpent.
roots_lines: Hebrew darak (H1869) — to tread, march, bend (a bow by treading); the treading of the winepress in Isa 63:3.
Greek pateō (G3961) — to tread, trample; “he treadeth the winepress” (Rev 19:15) and treading on serpents (Luk 10:19).
The figure reaches back to Gen 3:15, where the Seed bruises the serpent's head underfoot — the first promise in Scripture.
usage: “I have trodden the winepress alone” — wrath as the Lord's own unassisted work.
“Power to tread on serpents and scorpions” — authority given, never native.
“The young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet” — the psalm behind the promise.

pos: v.t. & adj. (to unbind, to set free; rendering Hebrew pathach, nathar, Greek luō)
etymology: Saxon leas, free, unbound. The verb is the exact opposite of binding, and Scripture makes it the characteristic work of Christ upon whatever holds His people.
biblical_def: To loose is to undo a bond, and in Scripture the bonds Christ undoes are of four kinds. Death: “Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it” (Act 2:24) — the grave could not keep its knot tied on Him. The grave-clothes of others: at Lazarus's tomb, “he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes… Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go” (Joh 11:44) — Christ raises, and the church unwraps. Oppression: the fast God chooses is “to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke” (Isa 58:6). And the church's declarative authority: “whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Mat 16:19) — the keys of the kingdom, exercised in preaching and discipline, announcing on earth what heaven has settled. In every case the loosing is Christ's; the church is given a voice in it, never a licence over it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines loose as to untie or unbind, to free from any fastening, to relax, to release from imprisonment, and to set at liberty.
webster_full: LOOSE, v.t. To untie or unbind; to free from any fastening.
2. To relax; as, to loose the bands of wickedness.
3. To release from imprisonment; to liberate; to set at liberty.
4. To free from obligation.
5. To disengage; to detach.
scriptures: Act 2:24
Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it.
And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go.
Isa 58:6
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?
And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.
corruption_summary: Binding and loosing has been claimed as a power the church wields over heaven, and separately as a formula for commanding spirits — where the text gives a declarative authority that announces heaven's verdict rather than creating it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two claimants press on Matthew 16:19. Rome reads the keys as a jurisdiction lodged in a single office, dispensing and withholding what heaven must then ratify. Certain charismatic teachers read binding and loosing as a technique of spiritual warfare, spoken over demons, illness, or circumstances until the desired outcome is released. The Greek perfect construction points the other way in both cases: what is bound on earth shall have been bound in heaven. The church declares; heaven has already decided. The keys are the preaching of the gospel and the exercise of discipline, and they are given to the assembly, not to a technique or a throne.

Isaiah 58 keeps the doctrine from becoming abstract. The loosing God actually wants from His people is the undoing of bands His people themselves have tied — unjust burdens, withheld wages, a yoke laid on a neighbour — and He says plainly that fasting without it is worthless. A congregation confident of its authority to loose in heaven, while binding heavy burdens on the poor at its door, has read the passage exactly backwards.
roots_summary: Hebrew nathar (H5425), to loose or set free, and pathach (H6605), to open or unfasten; Greek luō (G3089), to loose, untie, dissolve — the verb of resurrection and of the keys.
roots_lines: Hebrew nathar (H5425) — to loose, set free; “to loose the bands of wickedness” (Isa 58:6).
Greek luō (G3089) — to loose, untie, release, dissolve; the loosed pains of death (Act 2:24) and the loosing of Mat 16:19.
The same verb is used of dissolving the works of the devil (1Jn 3:8) — Christ came to untie what Satan tied.
usage: “Having loosed the pains of death” — the grave could not hold its knot.
“Loose him, and let him go” — Christ raises; the church unwraps.
“To loose the bands of wickedness” — the fast God actually chooses.

pos: v.t. (to keep safe, to guard from harm; rendering Hebrew shamar, natsar, Greek sōzō, tēreō)
etymology: From Latin præ, before, and servare, to keep. Preservation is the doctrine that God does not merely begin a thing — He keeps it.
biblical_def: Preservation is the second half of every promise God makes, and Scripture never leaves it to the creature. The pilgrim psalm states it twice in one breath: “The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul” (Psa 121:7). David prays for it as a man with no other resource: “Preserve me, O God: for in thee do I put my trust” (Psa 16:1). Paul, awaiting execution and abandoned by his friends, states it as settled fact: “the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom: to whom be glory for ever and ever” (2Ti 4:18) — note that he expected to die and still expected to be preserved, because preservation is measured by arrival in the kingdom, not by escape from the sword. And Proverbs shows the ordinary means God uses: “Discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee” (Pro 2:11) — wisdom is not an alternative to divine keeping but one of its instruments. This is the ground of the perseverance of the saints. They persevere because they are preserved.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines preserve as to keep or save from injury or destruction, to defend from evil, to uphold, and to keep in a sound state.
webster_full: PRESERVE, v.t. To keep or save from injury or destruction; to defend from evil.
2. To uphold; to sustain; to keep from failing or decaying.
3. To save from decay by the use of proper preservatives.
4. To keep or defend from corruption; as, to preserve youth from vice.
scriptures: The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul.
Psa 16:1
Michtam of David. Preserve me, O God: for in thee do I put my trust.
And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom: to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
Pro 2:11
Discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee:
corruption_summary: Preservation is confused with protection from hardship, so a believer who suffers concludes that God failed to keep him — when Paul used the word from a cell, expecting to die.
corruption_paragraphs: The promise that the LORD shall preserve thee from all evil is regularly heard as a guarantee of comfortable circumstances, and it collapses at the first hospital bill. Read the psalm through and its own measure appears: the LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore. The horizon is evermore; the object is the soul. Paul's use in 2 Timothy is decisive because his circumstances were terminal — the Lord will preserve me unto His heavenly kingdom, written by a man about to be executed. Preservation is safe arrival, not a smooth road.

The opposite error empties the doctrine from the other side, turning perseverance into a bare assurance that once one has professed faith nothing further matters. The Confession will not have it: the saints persevere because they are preserved, and the preservation shows itself in continuing. Proverbs supplies the ordinary machinery — discretion, understanding, a man's daily prudence — which God uses as genuinely as He uses angels. Trusting the Preserver and using discretion are the same obedience, not competing ones.
roots_summary: Hebrew shamar (H8104), to keep, guard, watch over, and natsar (H5341), to preserve; Greek tēreō (G5083), to keep or guard — the vocabulary of the keeping God.
roots_lines: Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard, watch; the repeated verb of Psalm 121, six times in eight verses.
Hebrew natsar (H5341) — to watch, guard, preserve; “Preserve me, O God” (Psa 16:1).
Greek tēreō (G5083) — to keep, guard, observe; kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation (1Pe 1:5).
usage: “He shall preserve thy soul” — the object of the promise named exactly.
“Will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom” — written by a man expecting execution.
“Discretion shall preserve thee” — the ordinary means God uses to do it.
